w: Neo-Byzantine domes rise over 3,170 square metres of floor space here — room for 5,000 worshippers, and until the year 2000 the largest finished Orthodox cathedral anywhere. As seat of the Patriarch of Bulgaria and the city's default postcard image, it is Sofia distilled into one building.
s: Sofia's postcard cathedral, once world's largest Orthodox
_facts: Cathedral church of the Patriarch of Bulgaria
One of the largest Christian church buildings by volume in the world; occupies 3,170 sq m, holds 5,000 worshippers
Believed to have been the largest finished Orthodox cathedral until the year 2000

w: Long before it was Sofia, this ground was Serdica, the Roman city whose name never quite left. It survives today both in the Serdica Fortress ruins at the city centre and in Serdika, the district built over the old Roman footprint — history layered right under the modern pavement.
s: Roman Sofia, buried under its own name
_facts: Serdica (or Sardica) was the historical Roman city on the site of today's Sofia
Its name survives in the Serdica Fortress in the city centre
Also the source of the name of the modern Serdika administrative district

w: Everyone in Sofia calls it simply the Russian Church, though its full name honours St Nicholas the Miracle-Worker. Standing on Tsar Osvoboditel Boulevard, it belongs to the Russian Orthodox Church rather than the Bulgarian one — foreign ground planted in the middle of the capital's central boulevard.
s: A slice of Russian Orthodoxy on Sofia's high street
_facts: Officially the Church of St Nicholas the Miracle-Maker
Russian Orthodox church in central Sofia

w: Built in the early twentieth century over natural mineral springs — and replacing an older Turkish bath on the same spot — this landmark served as Sofia's public bathhouse until 1986. It still stands downtown, testament to a capital that was, quite literally, built on hot water.
s: A bathhouse landmark over Sofia's hot springs
_facts: Landmark building in the city centre, near Sofia's mineral springs
Built in the early 20th century, near a former Turkish bath (since destroyed)
Used as the city's public baths until 1986

n: Saint Petka of the Saddlemakers Church
w: One of the odder church commutes in Europe: this medieval Bulgarian Orthodox chapel sits half-sunk below street level, reachable only by cutting through a shopping mall and down into the Serdika metro station concourse. Faith and consumer traffic, sharing the same stairwell.
s: Medieval church buried inside a metro mall
_facts: Medieval Bulgarian Orthodox church in central Sofia
Located in a semi-submerged shopping mall
Accessed via the Serdika metro station
